title: Infosys Bets on Trust as AI Reprices IT Services, Forrester Says
excerpt: Forrester says the IT services repricing has 12-24 months to run, and Infosys is declining uneconomic contracts rather than bidding on AI productivity it has not yet delivered.
body:
• Forrester says IT services is in a repricing that has another 12-24 months to run, as clients fold expected AI productivity gains into contracts at renewal.
  • Infosys told its last earnings call it had declined contracts whose economics did not work; constant-currency revenue grew 2.4% year on year in the quarter to June, full-year guidance was narrowed to 1.5-3%, and operating margin held at around 21%.
  • One European bank client raised its expected productivity gain from 25% by 2028 to 40% by end of this year, while creating new AI work, including a 3-5 year mainframe modernisation with Infosys and AWS.
  • For IT professionals and buyers: judge bids on productivity already demonstrated, not assumed - ask which gains are proven, which are assumptions, and how quality is protected if assumptions fail.

Infosys is positioning trust, not the lowest price, as its answer to an AI-driven repricing of IT services, according to a Forrester analysis of the company's 25th Confluence event in EMEA, held in Geneva. Salil Parekh opened the event by describing Infosys as a delivery organisation whose foundation is client trust, Forrester said - with no claim that the autonomous enterprise is near.

A repricing that is not finished

Forrester estimates the repricing has another 12-24 months to run and may be close to its peak. Clients at every stage of AI maturity are asking providers for productivity gains, and those gains are being written into contracts as they come up for renewal. Some providers, the firm warned, appear to be bidding below what they can realistically deliver, pricing in productivity their own delivery has not yet achieved.

That may win accounts short-term, Forrester argued, but it is less clear what it does to service quality two or three years into those contracts. Infosys said on its last earnings call that it had declined contracts whose economics did not work.

"IT services companies will play an even more critical role in the AI era. While AI agents can automate tasks and enhance productivity, enterprises still require deep systems integration, governance, trust frameworks, and large-scale transformation capabilities."

- Nandan Nilekani, Co-founder and Chairman, Infosys

One bank, both sides of the shift

A major European bank, a long-standing Infosys client, illustrated both pressures in a single account. The bank chose Infosys as a strategic partner after announcing its strategy in June 2023, with Infosys taking over the bank's IT centre in India. Its chief operating officer said the bank first raised its expected productivity gain in technology development to 25% by 2028 and now expects to reach 40% by the end of this year.

Under an effort-based contract, those gains press down the cost of delivering the work; whether total contract value grows depends on how much the bank reinvests. The same account is also generating new work: with Infosys and AWS, the bank is translating mainframe applications into natural language and then onto new platforms, application by application, over perhaps 3-5 years. It also runs an AI innovation lab with Infosys built around proof of value, not proof of concept.

Delivery rebuilt around people, software and tokens

Infosys is redesigning delivery around people, proprietary software and tokens - the units of AI model usage it pays for. Its workforce is shifting toward specialists who combine domain knowledge with engineering skills, organised in product-oriented delivery teams, or PODs.

Forrester identified three constraints on scaling that model: securing expertise training alone cannot supply, making the right technology bets as value moves from models to the harnesses around them, and the client's own pace of change. Infosys's technology answer is Infosys Topaz Fabric, an open stack on which clients can build and run their own agents using whichever agent framework they choose.

That platform sits inside the AI First value framework Infosys unveiled earlier this year, organised into six value pools including AI Trust, Process AI and Agentic Legacy Modernization. Infosys said it addresses an incremental AI-first opportunity of $300-400 billion by 2030, citing a Nasscom-McKinsey report, and that it works with 90% of its top 200 clients on AI, with more than 4,600 AI projects underway.

What to watch

Forrester said it is too early to know whether the stance will pay off. The signals it will watch: AI-first revenue moving toward 25-30% from 8%, margins holding, rejected accounts returning after lower-priced winners struggle, and organic growth recovering faster than peers once the repricing runs its course.

For the large Indian IT workforce in the US and elsewhere, the shift is practical: roles are moving toward domain-plus-engineering specialists who can build and govern agents, away from effort-based work that AI clauses are repricing. For buyers, Forrester advises a second look at any bid far below the incumbent's estimate - someone eventually pays for the gap, usually through service quality and renegotiations.
